analysis.one_liner: Requires the same minimum safety standards for all airline operations, including smaller commuter aircraft.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to committee, sent to its Aviation Subcommittee in February 1995, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Federal Aviation Administration to apply its minimum airline safety standards uniformly to every air carrier, no matter how small the aircraft. Today, smaller commuter planes can operate under looser standards. The bill allowed limited exceptions for very small aircraft (nine passengers or fewer), unscheduled small aircraft (up to 30 passengers), and older 19-seat aircraft whose design could not meet the uniform rules, but only where the FAA found an equivalent level of safety.
analysis.who_benefits: Passengers flying on commuter and regional airlines, especially travelers in small communities who depend on smaller aircraft, because they would be protected by the same safety standards as passengers on large scheduled airlines.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would require FAA minimum safety standards to apply to all air carrier operations uniformly, without regard to the seating or payload capacity of the aircraft.
The FAA would have until March 1, 1996, to put the uniform standards in place, with narrowly limited exceptions for very small, unscheduled, and older small aircraft.

Exceptions for older 19-seat aircraft would be allowed only where the aircraft's approved design makes compliance with a specific uniform standard impossible, and only with an equivalent level of safety.
The CRS summary describes the bill as applying certain minimum safety standards uniformly to all air carrier operations regardless of aircraft size.

analysis.who_pays: Small commuter and regional airlines, which would bear the cost of meeting the same safety standards as large carriers — new equipment, training, and operating procedures — costs that could show up as higher fares or reduced service on thin routes.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would fall hardest on small carriers serving rural and small-community routes, which could respond with higher fares, less frequent flights, or route cutbacks.

The bill sets a hard deadline (March 1, 1996) for uniform standards and gives the FAA limited room to tailor rules, which critics could argue forces costly retrofits on older 19-seat aircraft even where risks differ; the bill's own carve-out for pre-1987 designs acknowledges that some older aircraft physically cannot meet the uniform standards.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Passengers on smaller aircraft get a uniform safety floor that closes a known gap between commuter operations and major airlines. The cost is real but narrow: higher operating costs for small carriers, which would flow to travelers and small communities as higher fares or thinner schedules. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how much looser commuter standards actually were in practice — a question the record here does not answer.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 1995, referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then its Aviation Subcommittee, and died there without ever coming up for a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. James Oberstar of Minnesota, the senior Democrat on the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, introduced the bill on January 19, 1995.
The House referred it to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the same day.
On February 2, 1995, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Aviation, where it stayed.
The bill drew no cosponsors and no further action for the rest of the 104th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Small commuter and regional airlines, which avoided the cost of meeting uniform safety standards, kept operating under the lighter rules that applied to smaller aircraft.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Small commuter airlines that avoided new costs

for.name: Rep. James L. Oberstar
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-MN), senior member of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require uniform FAA safety standards for all air carrier operations.

against.name: House Aviation Subcommittee
against.role: Subcommittee of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in February 1995 and took no further action, so it never reached a House vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors, and no vote was ever taken, so the record shows no pattern of support or opposition by party.

industries.note: The bill would require these carriers to meet the same minimum safety standards as large airlines, raising their operating costs. The record contains no stated industry position, but the lighter standards these carriers operate under are precisely what the bill removes, and passengers bear the safety gap.

industries.industry: Aircraft manufacturers of small commercial aircraft
industries.note: Tighter operating standards could increase demand for newer, better-equipped aircraft, but the bill's carve-out for pre-1987 19-seat designs spares manufacturers from retrofitting older aircraft. The effect on this industry is modest and the record does not address it directly.
